lesson.title: Estimating a Mean When Sigma Is Unknown: The One-Sample T-Interval
lesson.summary: A one-sample t-interval estimates a population mean using the sample mean plus or minus a margin of error built from a t critical value and the standard error of the sample mean.
lesson.body:
A one-sample t-interval follows the same general template as every confidence interval you have built so far: statistic plus or minus critical value times standard error. Here the statistic is the sample mean, xbar, and because the population standard deviation sigma is unknown, the standard error is estimated using the sample standard deviation s, giving SE = s / square root of n. The critical value is a t critical value, t*, found using degrees of freedom n - 1 and the desired confidence level, exactly as covered in the previous section. Putting the pieces together, a one-sample t-interval is xbar plus or minus t*(s / square root of n).

Suppose a quality control inspector weighs a random sample of 12 cereal boxes from a production line and finds a sample mean weight of xbar = 16.35 ounces with a sample standard deviation of s = 0.4 ounces. Construct a 95 percent confidence interval for the true mean weight of all boxes from this line. Degrees of freedom is n - 1 = 11, so, from the previous section, t* = 2.201. The standard error is 0.4 divided by the square root of 12, which is 0.4/3.464 = 0.1155. The margin of error is t* times SE: 2.201(0.1155) = 0.254. The confidence interval is 16.35 plus or minus 0.254, which is (16.10, 16.60) ounces, rounding to two decimal places.

The correct interpretation is: we are 95 percent confident that the true mean weight of all cereal boxes produced on this line is between 16.10 and 16.60 ounces. This is a statement about the method, if this sampling and interval-building process were repeated many times, about 95 percent of the resulting intervals would capture the true population mean, not a statement about any one interval having a 95 percent chance of containing that fixed number. Like every procedure built on the t-distribution, though, this interval is only trustworthy if certain conditions about the data are met first, which is exactly what the next section checks.
